headline: mixed
texts: You have a solid base with some real gaps. Where you fell is information: it shows which model to fix, not what you cannot do. Start with the confident errors below, then the gaps, then the shaky areas, and retake the module after reviewing the cards.
Shaky: you know appendicitis is the commonest abdominal surgical emergency but wavered, perhaps swayed by graver conditions. Reread the qualifier in each stem.
Shaky: you know both causes but some age matches slipped. Link each to lymphoid tissue, which atrophies with age.
Shaky: the chain mostly holds but a step or the pain shift wobbled. Say the steps aloud: obstruction, pressure, congestion, arterial compromise, gangrene, perforation.
Shaky: you know the order but missed using it on a vignette. Ask 'what came first?' on every abdominal story.
Shaky: most signs are right but one pairing slipped. Rehearse the three side by side: Rovsing LIF press, psoas extension, obturator rotation.
Shaky: the score is partly there. Only RIF tenderness and leucocytosis score 2; re-add a case from the table to check.
Shaky: the imaging ladder is mostly right but a patient group slipped. Ask who the patient is, then name the rung.
Shaky: you have part of this. Check pregnancy first in reproductive-age women and list one look-alike per age group.
Shaky: you know both options but a qualifier slipped. Antibiotics-first needs CT-proven uncomplicated disease without an appendicolith.
Shaky: the ladder mostly holds but one rung slipped. Mass: Ochsner-Sherren; abscess: percutaneous drainage; interval surgery now selective.
Shaky: one list leaked into the other or the nerve wavered. Ask 'disease or knife?' for each complication.
Secure: carcinoid is the commonest appendix tumour and you know the 2 cm rule.

You swapped the two hip manoeuvres at first, then corrected. Extension of the hip is psoas; internal rotation of the flexed hip is obturator. Under exam pressure the names can flip again, so say the movement first, then the name.

You first attached the signs to the wrong positions, then rebuilt them. Psoas goes with retrocaecal, obturator and right rectal tenderness with pelvic. When rushed, ask which organ the appendix is touching.
You reversed Rovsing's sign at first, then fixed it. Pressure in the left iliac fossa causes pain in the right. Under time pressure, narrate it as 'press here, hurts there' before choosing.

You started from the end picture, then corrected the chain. Obstruction raises pressure, congestion and arterial compromise follow, then gangrene and perforation; pain starts periumbilical and shifts. In a cold stem, say the steps aloud in order.
You first put vomiting ahead of pain, then corrected. In appendicitis pain comes first; vomiting first points to gastroenteritis. Keep pain-first as a quick filter when a story seems off.

You misplaced the 2-point items or the meaning of the cut-off, then rebuilt them. Only RIF tenderness and leucocytosis score 2, out of 10; 7 or more is likely, not proof. Re-add from the table when numbers appear in an exam.
You first took a negative ultrasound as the end of the work-up, then corrected. In an adult, an unhelpful scan leads on to contrast CT, which is more accurate. Keep that next-step reflex.
You first gave CT to a child or pregnant patient, then corrected. Ultrasound comes first in both; CT is the adult answer. When a stem names age or pregnancy, circle it before choosing.

You first put MRI at the top of the pregnancy ladder, then corrected. Ultrasound is the first rung; MRI without gadolinium is used when ultrasound is inconclusive. Remember accuracy is not the only criterion for a first test.

You first answered from the older ultrasound key, then corrected. Older keys favoured ultrasound; current practice is ultrasound first in children and pregnancy, CECT most accurate in adults. Keep both as a pair.
You first skipped or delayed the pregnancy test, then corrected. Ectopic pregnancy changes both imaging and surgery, so test first. Under pressure, the favoured diagnosis can crowd this step out.

You first picked a more dramatic emergency, then corrected. Appendicitis is the commonest abdominal surgical emergency, including non-obstetric in pregnancy. Read the qualifier word before the options.

You first called a look-alike appendicitis, then corrected. Mittelschmerz fits young women with brief mid-cycle pain; caecal carcinoma fits an older man with a mass and anaemia. Keep generating look-alikes for each group.

You first gave the cause for the wrong age group, then corrected. Lymphoid hyperplasia predominates in children and young people; a faecolith in adults. Tie it to lymphoid tissue that atrophies with age.

You first merged the two complication lists, then rebuilt them. Disease: perforation, mass, abscess, pylephlebitis. Operation: wound infection (commonest), faecal fistula, stump appendicitis. Ask 'disease or knife?' for each item.
You first named a neighbouring nerve, then corrected. The ilioinguinal nerve is injured by a gridiron incision, leading to right inguinal hernia. Draw it on the site if it wobbles.
You first held that surgery is the only option, then corrected. Appendicectomy is the treatment of choice; antibiotics-first is accepted for selected uncomplicated cases. Give both in an exam answer.

You first offered antibiotics-first too widely, then corrected. It suits CT-proven uncomplicated disease without an appendicolith; an appendicolith predicts failure. Keep the three conditions together.

You first applied interval surgery to everyone, then corrected. Traditionally it was done at 6-8 weeks; now it is selective, with colonoscopy or CT in older patients to exclude caecal carcinoma. Under pressure, remember the older-patient work-up.
You first chose surgery up front, then corrected. A mass gets the Ochsner-Sherren regimen; a drainable abscess gets image-guided percutaneous drainage with antibiotics. Know when the regimen stops.
You tend to pair items correctly in form but attach them to the wrong partner. Rebuild the pair from the anatomy it depends on rather than recalling the pair.
You tend to run a sequence or direction backwards, starting from the end picture. Narrate the process cause first, 'press here, hurts there' or 'blockage, then pressure'.
You tend to start with the favoured diagnosis and skip the step that comes first. Ask 'what first, and why' before committing to a plan.
You tend to treat the first or most accurate test as the whole pathway. Think in rungs: what comes first, what comes after an unhelpful result.
You tend to drop the qualifier, such as age, pregnancy or appendicolith, and apply a general answer. Circle the patient detail before looking at the options.
You tend to answer from a remembered past-paper key without checking current practice. In such stems, give the old key and the modern view as a pair.
You tend to read a qualifier or a pattern too narrowly: 'most common' as 'most serious', or a classic picture as the only one. Underline the qualifier, then ask what else fits.

You tapped Sure on at least two answers that were wrong. Those are the costly ones, because you stop checking. Before tapping Sure, name the qualifier or the rule you are relying on; if you cannot, tap Guessing.

You used no hints and still fell into traps. Hints on the questions you were unsure about would have flagged the qualifier. Next time, open one before a stem with an age, a pregnancy or an exam-key flavour.

Review the cards in the order shown: confident errors first, then gaps, then shaky. Do two or three per sitting, answer before reading, then retake this module in about a week to see which models have changed.
